title: Workflows: research, review panel and parallel attempts

story: Two weeks into the pilot, a harder ticket fails its first attempt: after an hour the locked checks are still red. Someone on the team has an idea. Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, can already start many agents from inside its VM with a dynamic workflow, the script you wrote in the lesson on many agents. Why not start three agents that each try a fix at the same time, and keep the best one?

They try it on a copy of RH-1234. The three agents share one checkout, so all three edit ProjectsTable.tsx in the same minutes. The file becomes a mix of three ideas, each agent's tests run against the other agents' half-finished changes, and when a check finally passes, nobody can say whose change made it pass. More agents made things worse, not better.
hook.question: When Nova needs more agents, which ones can share one machine, and which ones each need a machine of their own?

p: Part of the confusion in the story is a word. Our platform has two kinds of workflow, and they live in different places. A Temporal workflow is code that runs on the orchestrator, outside every VM. ticketToPr is one: it starts once per ticket, survives restarts, waits days for people, claims and releases VMs, and is the only thing that may start a run. A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that Claude Code runs inside one session, inside one VM. It starts subagents, waits for them, and hands one result back to the session. It cannot claim a VM or start a run, because the VM has no route to the orchestrator.

So "use more agents" has two very different meanings. Inside the VM, a dynamic workflow adds agents that share that machine, its checkout and its session's permissions. On the orchestrator, a Temporal workflow can start more runs, each with its own machine and its own branch. This lesson's whole idea is choosing between them: agents that only read can share one machine, and agents that write each need their own.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the spike that comes first
p: Before Nova relies on dynamic workflows, a half-day spike runs one from the harness on a lite VM, under the same settings as a real run, and writes down what works. It checks that a headless session waits for the workflow and returns its result (if not, CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS=0 removes the wait ceiling), that every agent call goes through the gateway with the run's token and shows up in the result's modelUsage, that CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS caps the agents at 3, 6 or 12 by VM size, that saved workflows in the VM user's ~/.claude/workflows/ load by name, and that a stopped workflow can be relaunched with resumeFromRunId in the same session. The result is a one-page go or no-go for the research and review workflows.

Reading, searching and reviewing are jobs where extra agents help, because each one works alone and the results can be merged. Nova has two saved dynamic workflows for that. Before planning a bigger ticket, nova-research starts four cheap helpers on Haiku at the same time: where is the code, which merged PRs changed the same area, which tests cover it, and what our team's knowledge base says. Each returns file:line pointers, so the planner gets a wide view for little cost. For a fuzzy ticket it goes further: three planners write a plan from different angles (the smallest safe change, risk first, the user first), and a judge picks one and borrows the best ideas from the others.

After the build, a bigger diff (roughly 300 changed lines, 8 or more files, or a risky area) gets nova-review-panel instead of a single reviewer: five lenses read the diff, and for every important finding a skeptic tries to prove it wrong, so the panel finds more and cries wolf less. The panel is started from the read-only reviewer session of the previous lesson, and a workflow's agents use their session's permissions, so none of them can edit a file. In both cases Nova decides when a workflow is worth it, guided by one line in its planning skill, and the harness never forces one. Each is kept only if the eval bench says it helps.

read.h: Writers each get their own machine
p: Writing code is different, as the story showed: two writers in one checkout get in each other's way. But several independent tries really do help on hard problems; Anthropic raised Claude's score on the SWE-bench coding benchmark from 77.2% to 82.0% by running several attempts and letting tests pick one. So for a ticket the plan marks hard, or after a failed attempt, the Temporal workflow runs parallel attempts: two or three child workflows, named nova:RH-1234:a1, a2 and a3, each with its own full VM and its own branch, each building from the same approved plan and the same locked checks. A child workflow is a workflow started by another workflow, which waits for its result.

The parent waits for all of them with Promise.allSettled, not Promise.all, so one attempt whose VM died does not fail the whole ticket. It drops every attempt that fails a locked QA check or breaks other tests. If more than one survives, a judge (Opus at medium effort) reads the ticket, the surviving diffs and their check results side by side, never the transcripts, and picks one. Only the winner goes on to self-review, the PR and Byte, so one change ships, and the other attempts' VMs are released. Each attempt takes one of Nova's three VM slots, so attempts wait in line instead of starving other tickets, and the default is two attempts while the warm pool is small.

notes.text: One try only in the lab, so a dead VM shows up at once. The real policy is the long preset with heartbeats.
allSettled waits for every attempt and never throws, so one failure cannot fail the ticket.
Each child is named after the parent plus its attempt: nova:RH-1234:a1. One name, one run, as always.
Its own branch per attempt. In the real platform it also claims its own full VM.
Survivors pass the locked checks and the wider verify run. Anything else is dropped.
The lab keeps the first survivor. The Build step replaces this line with a stand-in for the judge.

lab.title: Three attempts, one winner
needs: About 150 MB of disk for the Temporal packages
lab.goal: Run parallel attempts as Temporal child workflows, see one attempt die without failing the ticket, and pick a winner from the survivors.

guess.q: The parent starts three attempts and waits for them with Promise.allSettled. Attempt a1 breaks a neighbouring test, a2 passes everything, and a3's VM dies twice. What does the parent return?

options.why: That is what Promise.all would do. allSettled waits for all three and reports each one's outcome instead of throwing.

options.text: a2 as the winner, with a1 dropped and one failed attempt.
options.why: a3 failed, a1 finished but broke a test, and a2 is the only survivor, so no judge is needed.
Speed does not matter. Only an attempt that passes the locked checks and the wider tests can win.

lab.build: Give the parent a judge. In activities.mjs, change a3's outcome so it passes everything with a smaller diff: { lockedChecksPass: true, verifyPass: true, changedLines: 37, note: "all checks pass, with a smaller diff" }. Now two attempts survive. In workflows.mjs, replace const winner = survivors[0] with a stand-in for the judge that picks the survivor with the fewest changed lines. Restart the worker (Ctrl+C, then node worker.mjs) and run node start.mjs again.
checks: node start.mjs returns winner a2, branch nova/RH-1234-a2, failed 1 and dropped [ 'a1' ].
temporal workflow list shows the parent nova:RH-1234 and three children ending in :a1, :a2 and :a3, with :a3 Failed.
describe on nova:RH-1234:a3 shows the message a3: the VM died twice.
After your change, node start.mjs returns winner a3, failed 0 and dropped [ 'a1', 'a2' ].
You stopped the worker and the dev server with Ctrl+C.

solution.text:
// stand-in for the judge, which reads the ticket, the diffs and the check results side by side
  const winner = survivors.reduce((best, a) => (a.changedLines < best.changedLines ? a : best));

lab.fix: Someone found Promise.allSettled hard to read and changed it to Promise.all, mapping the values into the same shape. The next hard ticket lost an hour of work: one attempt's VM died, the whole parent failed with WorkflowFailedError, and the attempt that had passed every check was thrown away with it. Make that change, restart the worker, run node start.mjs to see the WorkflowFailedError, then put allSettled back.

check.q: Nova wants three agents to look for where the code of a fuzzy ticket lives. Where should they run?

options.text: As three Temporal child workflows, each with its own VM
options.why: Three machines for three readers would cost a lot for nothing. Readers do not get in each other's way.

options.text: In a dynamic workflow inside Nova's own VM
options.why: Reading can be shared: the helpers search the same checkout and return pointers, and only the merged result reaches the planner.

options.text: As three new runs started from inside the VM
options.why: The VM has no route to the orchestrator. Only the orchestrator starts runs.

check.q: Why do parallel attempts each get their own VM and branch?

options.text: Because each attempt writes code, and writers in one checkout mix their changes so no test can say which idea worked
options.why: Isolation is what makes the attempts comparable. Each one is judged on its own branch by the same locked checks.

options.text: Because Temporal allows only one child workflow per VM
options.why: Temporal knows nothing about VMs. The reason is about writing code, not about Temporal.

options.text: Because the warm pool has machines to spare
options.why: It does not: each attempt takes one of Nova's slots, which is why the default is two attempts.

check.q: Two attempts survive the locked checks. What decides which one ships?

options.why: Speed says nothing about quality. Both passed the same checks.

options.text: Both are opened as PRs and the reviewers choose
options.why: Only one change ships, and people should not be asked to review two versions of one ticket.

options.text: A judge that reads the ticket, both diffs and their check results, but not the transcripts
options.why: The judge compares the work, not the stories the agents told themselves. Then only the winner goes to self-review and the PR.

p: The two saved dynamic workflows, nova-research.js and nova-review-panel.js, live in ai-agents/harness/workflows/ and are baked into the VM user's ~/.claude/workflows/ by Packer. Workflow is in Nova's allowedTools so it runs under dontAsk, CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS is 3, 6 or 12 by VM size, and the research workflow's plan schema, passed in as args.planSchema, must be converted with target: "draft-7" like every other schema. The spike's settings sketch passes settings as a JSON string; passing the object lets TypeScript check the keys.

Parallel attempts are a stretch goal: an attempts block in ticketToPr that runs buildAttempt children named nova:<key>:a1 to a3 with Promise.allSettled, drops attempts that fail a locked check or the verify command, and asks an Opus 5.5 judge to pick. Each attempt takes a Nova slot, all attempts share the ticket's cost tag and backstop, and the block is kept only if pass@1 on the five big and the hardest TICKET-BENCH tasks rises enough to pay for the extra VMs. The run's broker scope must name each attempt's branch (nova/RH-1234-a1 and so on), because the broker pushes only to branches the scope names.

tickets.why: The spike: does a dynamic workflow run headless in a lite VM behind the gateway?
nova-research: parallel readers before planning, and three plans with a judge for fuzzy tickets.
nova-review-panel for bigger diffs, and the skill line on when to fan out.
Parallel attempts as Temporal child workflows, each with its own VM, and a judge that picks one.

words.plain: Durable code on the orchestrator, such as ticketToPr; the only thing that claims VMs and starts runs.
A JavaScript script Claude Code runs inside one session in one VM, starting subagents that share that machine.
A Temporal workflow started by another workflow, which waits for its result.
Two or three independent tries at a hard ticket, each on its own VM and branch; tests and a judge pick one.
Waits for every promise and reports each outcome, without failing when one of them fails.

review.q: From memory: one sentence each on what a Temporal workflow and a dynamic workflow are, and where each one runs.
review.a: A Temporal workflow is durable code on the orchestrator (ticketToPr) that claims VMs and starts runs. A dynamic workflow is a script Claude Code runs inside one session in one VM; it starts subagents that share the machine and cannot start runs.

review.q: A teammate wants the review panel for every PR, "because more reviewers find more". What do you answer?
review.a: On small diffs it only adds cost. The panel is for bigger diffs (around 300 lines, 8+ files or a risky area); Nova decides from a skill line, and the panel stays only if the bench shows it finds real issues without more false alarms.

review.q: Why must the attempts be compared by a judge that reads diffs and check results, not transcripts?
review.a: A transcript is the agent's own story about its work and can be persuasive without being right. The diff and the check results are facts the judge can compare side by side.

remember: Readers can share one VM through a dynamic workflow; writers each need their own VM through Temporal, and the tests and a judge pick the one change that ships.
